directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I don’t have the ability to execute `git` commands or write files directly into your local filesystem from here, so I’ll walk you through what you’d normally do step‑by‑step and give you ready‑to‑paste templates for each artifact.  

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub (or use HTTPS)
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artifacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Open the folder in your editor or list the files:

```bash
tree -L 2   # shows two levels deep
```

Typical Node.js repos contain:

| File | Typical purpose |
|------|-----------------|
| `package.json` | Dependencies + scripts |
| `app.js` or `index.js` | Entry point |
| `.env.example` | Sample env vars |
| `Dockerfile` | Container definition |
| `k8s/*.yaml` | Deployment manifests |
| `.github/workflows/*` | CI/CD pipelines |

Look at `package.json` to see the start script (`npm start`) and the port the app listens on (often `process.env.PORT || 3000`). If there’s no explicit port, assume `3000`.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a new file named **`Dockerfile`** in the repo root with the following content (adjust the base image if you want a newer one):

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies first (cached layer)
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Build step (if needed – e.g., transpile TypeScript)
# RUN npm run build

# Runtime stage
FROM node:18-alpine AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV production
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy only built artifacts from builder
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app ./

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "app.js"]   # adjust if entry point differs
```

> **Tip:** If the repo uses Yarn, replace `npm` with `yarn` and adjust the install line accordingly.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s` (if it doesn’t exist) and inside it create `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with actual registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: PORT
          value: "3000"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort or ClusterIP as needed
```

> Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with your container registry URL (e.g., `ghcr.io/your-org/nodejs-welcome`).

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Inside `.github/workflows/`, create `ci-cd.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # required for pushing to GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ hashFiles('**/Dockerfile') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you have a cluster context set
      # uses: azure/k8s-set-context@v2
      # with:
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
      #   method: manual
      #   config-data: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
      #
      # - name: Apply manifests
      #   run: |
      #     kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

> **Important:**  
> * Ensure you have a secret named `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` in the repo settings if you want automatic deployments.  
> * The workflow above pushes to GitHub Packages; modify the registry/tag logic if you’re using Docker Hub or another registry.

---

## 3️⃣ Add, commit, and push the changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions pipeline"
git push origin main
```

If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 4️⃣ Verify

* Check the Actions tab on GitHub → you should see a successful run.  
* After the image is pushed, you can inspect it via `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome`.  
* If you enabled the optional deploy step, verify the pod status:

```bash
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
kubectl logs <pod-name>
```

That’s it! Once the pipeline passes, every future push to `main` will rebuild, repush, and optionally redeploy your Node.js app.
